items.title: The cognition of dynamic evaluation of operating room environmental quality among medical staff: a qualitative study
items.abstract: Objective This qualitative study, guided by the Donabedian three-dimensional quality model, aimed to explore the real perceptions of multidisciplinary healthcare professionals regarding the dynamic evaluation of the operating room environment quality. The ultimate goal was to identify current management deficiencies and propose evidence-based strategies for optimization. Method Using a descriptive qualitative design with a hybrid analytic orientation, purposive sampling recruited 7 operating-room nurses, 6 surgeons, 5 anesthesiologists, and 2 infection-control specialists from 4 tertiary Grade A hospitals. After ethics approval, formal semi-structured interviews were conducted in March 2026. Interview data were transcribed, manually coded, and analyzed in NVivo 15.0 using Colaizzi's method. The Donabedian model informed the interview guide and later organization of evaluation-related categories. Results Three core themes were extracted: (1) the four-dimensional connotation of operating-room environmental quality, comprising physical, chemical, biological, and humanistic dimensions; (2) nine preliminary candidate indicators for dynamic evaluation, grouped across structure, process, and outcome domains; and (3) healthcare professionals' perceptions of potential safety and health implications for staff and patients. These findings highlight a gap between current static monitoring practices and the dynamic nature of intraoperative environmental risks. Conclusion Participants' accounts suggest that a preliminary candidate framework for dynamic evaluation could incorporate structural conditions, process monitoring, and outcome-related feedback. Integrated management that considers both occupational health and patient safety represents a practice implication to be empirically evaluated. This study provides a qualitative foundation for subsequent Delphi consultation and psychometric or empirical validation of a dynamic OR environmental assessment framework.

items.title: The Dark Side of Generative AI in Marketing: AI-Generated False and Misleading Advertising and Its Consumer Consequences
items.abstract: Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming advertising by enabling marketers to create persuasive text, images, and other promotional content rapidly and at lower cost. At the same time, the ability of generative systems to produce highly realistic content creates concerns about deception, misinformation, transparency, and the credibility of consumer-facing information. The present study examines the consumer consequences of AI-generated false and misleading advertising, with particular emphasis on hallucinated product claims. The study focuses on whether AI-generated hallucinated product claims influence perceived deception, AI skepticism, and perceived information reliability, and whether these consumer responses subsequently shape purchase intention. Drawing on the stimulus-organism-response (S-O-R) framework, the study conceptualizes hallucinated product claims as the stimulus, the three consumer evaluations as the organism, and purchase intention as the response. A quantitative, cross-sectional, deductive research design was adopted. Data were collected from 320 business-school students and faculty members through a structured questionnaire using a five-point Likert scale, and the model was assessed using SmartPLS. The reported measurement results show Cronbach's alpha values above 0.70, composite reliability above the stated threshold, and average variance extracted above 0.50 for all constructs, indicating acceptable reliability and convergent validity. The reported discriminant-validity matrix also supports construct distinctiveness. The structural model reports a VIF range of 1.47-2.24 and an R² of 0.421 for purchase intention. Four of the six hypotheses are supported. AI-generated hallucinated product claims significantly increase perceived deception and significantly reduce perceived information reliability. Perceived deception significantly reduces purchase intention, while perceived information reliability significantly increases purchase intention. The paths from hallucinated product claims to AI skepticism and from AI skepticism to purchase intention are not statistically significant. The findings indicate that message-level judgments of deception and information reliability are more consequential for purchase intention in the reported model than generalized skepticism toward AI. The study extends the S-O-R perspective to the dark side of GenAI in advertising and highlights the importance of factual verification, transparency, human oversight, disclosure, and consumer AI literacy. Keywords: Generative artificial intelligence; AI hallucinations; misleading advertising; perceived deception; AI skepticism; perceived information reliability; purchase intention; stimulus-organism-response theory.

items.title: The Density of Thought: Predicting and Steering Reasoning in Large Language Models
items.abstract: We investigate whether variation in information density across chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning steps predicts answer correctness and can serve as a controllable inference-time target. We prompt frozen pretrained models to solve problems via CoT and measure the density of each reasoning step with two independent metrics: LP variance (how unevenly information is distributed across steps, computed as the variance in mean per-token negative log-likelihood) and the Caveman compression ratio. We then test whether density correlates with, and can be steered to improve, answer correctness. Experiments across six model scales, two training paradigms, and 60 GSM8K problems yield four main findings. First, lower LP variance predicts correctness in supervised fine-tuned (SFT) models, but this relationship weakens with scale and reverses in reinforcement-learning (RL) distilled models. Training paradigm therefore appears more influential than model size in determining density behaviour. Second, synthetic experiments reveal an intrinsic complexity preference: models trained on uniformly distributed data learn complexity-favouring distributions 2.0 to 2.6 times more accurately than simplicity-favouring ones. Third, direct inference-time density steering reduces accuracy from 60.0% to 8.3%, indicating that natural density patterns are functionally important to reasoning. Fourth, pre-generation nudging combining hint injection with contrastive KV-cache steering improves accuracy by 13.3 percentage points, consistent across both metrics. Finally, we introduce Entropy-Gated Density Routing (EGDR), a self-supervised method using token-level Shannon entropy to gate proportional KVcache adjustments during generation, improving accuracy by 10.0 percentage points without any external guidance.

items.title: The Dual Edge of Digitalization: A Psychological Analysis of Motivation, Productivity, and Wellbeing using the Job Demands-Resources Model
items.abstract: The rapid and ubiquitous integration of Digital Information and Communication Technologies (DICT) into the modern workplace has fundamentally restructured organizational behavior, yielding unprecedented operational efficiencies while simultaneously introducing severe, novel psychological hazards. This exhaustive research paper critically analyzes the dual edge of digitalization through the theoretical lens of the extended Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model. By conceptualizing technological factors as either digital job demands or digital job resources, this analysis elucidates the complex, multi-directional pathways through which digitalization influences employee work engagement, motivation, productivity, and psychological wellbeing. Particular attention is devoted to technostress, the pervasive reach of algorithmic management (AM), and the recent, disruptive proliferation of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in knowledge work. The comprehensive synthesis of empirical literature, heavily supported by Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) data, reveals that while digital resources (e.g., temporal flexibility, algorithmic guidance, digital leadership) can trigger a motivational process leading to high engagement and thriving, digital demands (e.g., techno-overload, continuous availability, intense electronic monitoring, and verification fatigue) trigger a health impairment process characterized by cognitive depletion and burnout. Furthermore, this paper explores critical buffering mechanisms, notably Psychological Capital (PsyCap) and proactive digital job crafting, which empower employees to navigate the digital ecosystem autonomously. Ultimately, the paper provides evidence-based recommendations for organizations to mitigate digital strain by implementing "Right to Disconnect" policies, deploying human-centric AI, and establishing transparent algorithmic governance frameworks.

items.title: THE DUAL ROLE OF LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS IN CYBERSECURITY: THREATS, DEFENSES, AND RESEARCH DIRECTIONS
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs), have come in from three angles into the cybersecurity world. They're a new class of system that has to be secured, they are a capability that reduces the cost of offense, and they are a tool that enhances defense. Current reviews consider either of these directions only, making it hard for researchers and practitioners to glimpse the interplay of the three. This review collates research published from 2023–2026 in all three of the following, presented in the dual-use approach. We provide a three-layer taxonomy of attacks on LLM-based systems, which include attacks at the model layer (jailbreak, poisoning, extraction), the system layer (direct, indirect, and multimodal prompt injection, retrieval poisoning), and the agentic layer (memory poisoning, tool abuse, protocol exploits, and multimodal agent propagation). Then, we discuss the use of LLMs for attacking (phishing, social engineering, malware generation, autonomous attacks) and protecting (threat intelligence, intrusion detection, vulnerability detection and repair, security operations). We list the key defense families and the standards of measurement for them. There is a common theme in our synthesis: the reported success rates of similar threat classes vary from less than 10% to more than 87% in different benchmarks and experimental designs; threats are rarely tested against adaptive threats; and the security to utility trade-off is rarely quantified. We conclude with eight research directions: Multilingual Guardrail Robustness, Longitudinal Security Measurement and Human Factors in AI-assisted Security Operations.

items.title: The Effect of AI-Supported Coding Instruction on 21st-Century Skills
items.abstract: The purpose of this study is to examine the effect of artificial intelligence–supported coding instruction on students’ 21st-century skills. A quantitative research approach employing a pretest–posttest quasi-experimental design with a control group was used. The study group consisted of high school students. While the experimental group received artificial intelligence-supported coding instruction, the control group continued with coding instruction based on the existing teaching method. Data were collected using a 21st-century skills scale. To examine within-group changes, a paired-samples t test was conducted, and to determine between-group differences, ANCOVA was performed by controlling pretest scores. The findings indicated that both the experimental and control groups showed significant increases in their 21st-century skills scores. When pretest scores were controlled, no statistically significant difference was found between the posttest scores of students who received artificial intelligence–supported coding instruction and those who received coding instruction based on the existing teaching method. The results demonstrate that both the existing teaching method–based coding instruction and artificial intelligence–supported coding instruction are effective in developing students’ 21st-century skills. Accordingly, it is recommended that different instructional approaches used in coding education be planned in a way that supports targeted 21st-century skills and that teaching processes be structured using a holistic approach.

items.title: The Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Self-Regulated Learning: A Meta-Analysis
items.abstract: This meta-analysis systematically examined the effects of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) on students’ self-regulated learning (SRL), including its overall effectiveness and its impact on the cognitive, metacognitive, motivational, and behavioral dimensions of SRL. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, this study conducted a random-effects meta-analysis to synthesize evidence from 17 studies. The results revealed a statistically significant positive average effect of GenAI on SRL (Hedges’ g = 0.74). Nevertheless, substantial between-study heterogeneity suggested considerable variation in the magnitude of this effect across educational contexts. Positive average effects were also observed across the cognitive, metacognitive, motivational, and behavioral dimensions of SRL. However, a multilevel random-effects meta-analysis with CR2-robust inference indicated that effect sizes did not differ significantly across these dimensions (p = 0.564). Moderator analyses revealed significant differences in effect sizes associated with experimental design and intervention duration, whereas no significant differences were observed for subject domain, GenAI intervention type, GenAI tool, or personalization. Overall, the findings suggest that GenAI has the potential to contribute to the development of SRL, highlighting the importance of using GenAI as a scaffold to support, rather than replace, learners’ active self-regulatory processes.

items.title: The Energy Economics of Artificial Intelligence Data Centers: Demand Uncertainty, System Costs, Flexibility, and Credible Decarbonization
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is accelerating data center electricity demand, but annual energy totals alone do not reveal when, where, or at whose cost new loads enter power systems. This review asks how uncertain projects should be translated into demand, infrastructure, price, flexibility, and environmental consequences. We conducted a structured critical review of 44 peer-reviewed studies, working papers, and official, regulatory, statistical, system-operator, and institutional reports identified through 31 August 2026, with explicit source selection and claim-level reliability appraisal. The central finding is that the economic effect of AI data centers depends on project-realization probability, coincident demand, and location, not on announced capacity alone. Concentrated growth can require generation and network investment and raise local prices. Enforceable temporal or spatial flexibility can reduce these costs, but unverified flexibility warrants no planning credit. Annual renewable matching supports an accounting claim but not necessarily consequential decarbonization, which also requires additional supply, temporal matching, and geographic deliverability. Policy should therefore condition connection on project credibility, cost responsibility, measured flexibility, and credible procurement. This review’s incremental contribution is to move beyond consumption inventories by integrating uncertain project realization, short-run operation, medium-run connection and investment, long-run expansion, distributional incidence, and environmental counterfactuals in one energy-economics framework.

items.title: The Forgotten Student—Generative AI Use in Medical Education and the Technology-Integrated Educational Design (TIED) Road Map: Scoping Review
items.abstract: Abstract Background The growing impact of generative AI (GenAI) on medical education has given rise to many reviews discussing AI literacy, trustworthiness, potential uses, and institutional or faculty benefits. However, there has been surprisingly little review-level attention to its impact on students and learning. Objective This scoping review examines the impact of GenAI-enabled educational interventions on undergraduate medical students. Methods We followed the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines. An electronic search was conducted between September 22 and September 24, 2025, across Ovid (MEDLINE and Embase), PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus, with no language or date restrictions, and excluding reviews, commentaries, letters, editorials, preprints, conference papers, and study protocols. Each record was independently screened by two reviewers, who thoroughly discussed and agreed upon its final inclusion in the analysis. We used a modified version of the Kirkpatrick model as an analytical framework for the final dataset. Results Twenty-seven studies were included. Most were published in 2025 (n=21) and in the Journal of Medical Internet Research or its sister journals (n=9). The educational interventions described included GenAI used for simulated patient experiences, knowledge or decision support, and content generation. The majority of studies fell under Kirkpatrick level 1 (n=23), focusing on initial user reactions. The studies that fell under Kirkpatrick level 2 (n=16) examined learning outcomes in terms of knowledge gain, skill acquisition, and learning attitudes. No studies were classified as Kirkpatrick level 3. Three studies demonstrated explicit theoretical grounding and therefore were classified as Kirkpatrick level 4 in our modified model. Only 13 studies spanned across levels. Numerous studies fell outside the model, including studies without student-facing interventions (119 studies) and studies focused on GenAI performance (110 studies). Although these studies were not included in the final analysis, they revealed the extent to which other topics dominate the academic conversation on GenAI in medical education. Conclusions Our review highlights the volume of studies that prioritize tool performance over learning processes, as well as a trend toward the fragmentation of educational design elements in research evaluating GenAI-enabled educational interventions. Therefore, based on our findings, we developed the Technology-Integrated Educational Design (TIED) road map that reimagines the Kirkpatrick model as a tool to guide student-centered, theory-driven, and iterative design of technology-enabled educational interventions. By integrating preinstructional exploration, mechanism-oriented thinking, educational design, implementation, and evaluation within a single student-centered framework, the road map encourages educators and researchers to consider not only whether technology-enabled interventions work and are acceptable, but also how, for whom, and under what conditions they support meaningful learning.

items.title: The Future of AI, Education and Economics: Policy Recommendations for a Sustainable Knowledge Society
items.abstract: Three transformations are unfolding in India simultaneously, and this chapter argues that none of them can be fully understood, or wisely governed, in isolation from the other two. Artificial intelligence has moved, within a single decade, from a specialised research pursuit to a general-purpose technology reshaping how India teaches, works, and grows; the National Education Policy 2020 has committed the country to becoming a "knowledge society" through an ambitious, still-unfinished restructuring of school and higher education; and India's economic-policy establishment has begun treating AI-enabled growth and human-capital formation as a single connected project rather than two separate portfolios. This chapter synthesises evidence across all three domains - India's AI institutional architecture (the IndiaAI Mission, the National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence, and the 2026 India AI Impact Summit's New Delhi Declaration), NEP 2020's knowledge-economy targets (a fifty-per-cent higher-education Gross Enrolment Ratio by 2035, the National Credit Framework, and India's research-investment shortfall), and the international literature on AI, automation, and human capital formation - to assess how close India actually is to the "sustainable knowledge society" its own policy documents describe. It finds a pattern familiar from this volume's sector-specific chapters repeated here at macro scale: ambitious institutional design substantially outrunning measured, funded delivery, evident in an AI mission that has disbursed under four per cent of its five-year outlay and a research-and-development investment rate roughly a quarter of the level comparable innovation economies sustain. Rather than treating this gap as merely descriptive, the chapter closes with a dedicated set of policy recommendations addressed to the specific, evidenced shortfalls the preceding sections identify, arguing that closing the disbursement-and-delivery gap, not further expanding institutional ambition, is what now stands between India's stated knowledge-society vision and its realisation.

items.title: The Geo Ai Revolution: The Future of Geography in The Age of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Abstract The integration of artificial intelligence with geospatial technology has given rise to Geospatial Artificial Intelligence (GeoAI), fundamentally altering how geographical information is produced, analyzed, and applied. This paper examines whether GeoAI functions merely as an advanced analytical toolkit or constitutes a structural paradigm shift in spatial knowledge generation. Through a systematic literature synthesis, analytical scenario modeling, and empirical case studies, we demonstrate that Geography is transitioning from a human-driven descriptive field to a continuously computational, multimodal, and semi-autonomous spatial intelligence system. The development of geospatial foundation models (GeoFMs), autonomous GIS agents, and Earth digital twins signals a movement toward AI-native geographical workflows. To conceptualize this transformation, we propose the GeoAI Transformation of Geographical Intelligence Framework (GT-GIF). Looking toward 2050, the discipline may shift toward continuous Planetary Geographical Intelligence. However, human contextual reasoning, ethical oversight, fieldwork, and critical interpretation remain vital safeguards. Finally, the paper addresses the Global South perspective specifically focusing on India, by examining risks such as spatial bias, surveillance, and algorithmic colonialism alongside opportunities for climate resilience and sustainable development.

items.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Primary School Chinese Language Teaching: An Analysis from Teachers' Perspectives
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has entered Chinese primary education faster than curricula, assessment systems and teacher preparation have adapted to it. While a growing body of Chinese scholarship explores how GenAI can “empower” yuwen (Chinese language) teaching, considerably less attention has been paid to the disruptive effects that frontline teachers must absorb in daily practice. This article offers a qualitative, interpretive analysis of how AI affects primary school Chinese language teaching when viewed from the teacher’s position. Rather than collecting new empirical data, it analyses three bodies of material: national and international policy documents on GenAI in schools, Chinese and international research on AI in language and primary education, and published expert commentary on Chinese language education in the AI era. Read through the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, the analysis identifies four interrelated areas of impact: the erosion of foundational literacy practices such as character writing and sustained reading; a crisis of authorship in writing instruction, in which teachers are pushed from cultivating expression towards verifying authenticity; the reconfiguration of teachers’ professional roles and identities; and institutional ambiguity arising from gaps between national policy, school practice, assessment and home use. The article argues that the central difficulty is not technological access but a misalignment between AI-saturated learning environments and product-oriented teaching and assessment traditions. Implications are drawn for process-oriented writing pedagogy, assessment reform, teacher professional development and home–school collaboration.

items.title: The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking: Cognitive Scaffolding, Substitution, and the Risk of Deskilling
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has raised fundamental questions about its effects on critical thinking and cognitive development. Evidence from recent empirical studies suggests a dual pattern: structured forms of AI assistance can sustain users’ cognitive activity and enhance engagement and performance, whereas more substitutive forms of use are associated with reduced autonomous reasoning and poorer subsequent independent performance. This article argues that these findings can be understood by considering how cognitive work is distributed between users and AI systems and how this distribution may evolve over time. In particular, I examine a six-step sequence in which successful complementary assistance can increase trust and delegation; greater delegation can remain complementary or become increasingly substitutive; and increasingly substitutive interactions can reduce the autonomous exercise of critical thinking and potentially hinder the development or maintenance of critical-thinking capacities over time. The available evidence provides substantial support for the first five steps considered individually and substantial, though less direct, support for the sixth. The article concludes by discussing educational, design, and social implications, arguing that preserving cognitive agency requires fostering complementary rather than progressively substitutive forms of interaction.

items.title: The Impact of Generative AI on Geography Education and Map-Mapping Skills: Transforming Cartographic Learning, Spatial Thinking and the Future of Geographical Education
items.abstract: AbstractGenerative AI can now create maps, explain geographical concepts, generate spatial visualizations, assist GIS workflows, write code, interpret satellite imagery and transform natural-language instructions into geospatial outputs. This capability creates a fundamental educational question: if AI can increasingly perform tasks traditionally taught to geography students, what geographical skills should students learn in the future? This paper critically investigates this question through a systematic synthesis of emerging empirical evidence, theoretical frameworks and future scenarios. Drawing on studies of AI-assisted spatial thinking, GIS education, cartographic literacy and cognitive offloading, the paper argues that Generative AI may shift geography education from teaching students primarily how to produce maps toward teaching students how to critically conceptualize, validate, interrogate and ethically use AI-generated geospatial representations. The paper proposes an original conceptual framework—the Generative AI–Geography Education Transformation Model (GAIGETM)—and develops evidence-based 2030–2050 scenarios. It concludes that the future of geography education depends not on whether AI can make maps, but on whether educational systems can teach students to question, validate, interpret and critically reason about the maps that AI produces.

items.title: The Impact of Social Media Use on Musculoskeletal Pain and Mental Health Among Adolescents and Young Adults: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: Introduction: For teenagers and young adults, social media has become an essential part of everyday life. Social engagement, education, entertainment, and communication have all been revolutionized by platforms like Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, Snapchat, and X. However, extended usage of social media has sparked worries about one's physical and mental well-being. According to new research, excessive social media use may increase the risk of mental health issues like anxiety, depression, stress, and diminished psychological well-being while also contributing to musculoskeletal pain through bad posture and extended screen time. The purpose of this systematic review is to compile the information that is currently available about how social media use affects young adults' and adolescents' musculoskeletal pain and mental health. Methodology: The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) standards were used in conducting this systematic review. Studies published between 2015 and 2025 were found by searching electronic databases such as PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar. Included were studies assessing young adults' and adolescents' usage of social media, musculoskeletal complaints, and mental health outcomes. Narrative synthesis and data extraction were done. Results: Through database searching, 1,387 records in all were found. Twenty-four studies satisfied the inclusion criteria after screening and eligibility evaluation. Long-term usage of social media has been linked in the majority of studies to neck discomfort, shoulder pain, upper back pain, and bad posture. Furthermore, sadness, anxiety, stress, sleep problems, loneliness, and low self-esteem have all been repeatedly linked to excessive social media use. There is a dose-response association between screen time and hazards to one's physical and mental health, according to several research. Conclusion: Teenagers and young adults who use social media excessively have worse mental health outcomes as well as musculoskeletal pain. To lessen these health effects, activities to promote mental health, digital wellbeing, ergonomic awareness, and educational interventions are required.

items.title: The Importance of Electronic Communication in the Use of Artificial Intelligence Programs and Applications in the Field of Smart Agriculture from the Point of View of Agricultural Extension Workers in Nineveh Governorate, Iraq
items.abstract: The study aimed to identify the level of importance of electronic communication among agricultural extension workers in using artificial intelligence (AI) programs and applications in the field of smart agriculture. It also aimed to identify the most frequently used electronic communication means by extension workers in employing AI programs and applications and rank them according to their relative importance; measure the contribution of electronic communication to improving extension workers' efficiency in using AI programs and applications in smart agriculture; identify individual differences in the importance of electronic communication and the use of AI applications according to selected independent variables, namely gender, educational qualification, years of service, training courses, level of Internet use, and willingness to use social networking sites concerning smart-agriculture technologies; and identify the obstacles facing extension workers in using AI applications in smart agriculture. To obtain the study data, a questionnaire consisting of five parts was used. The first part concerned the respondents' personal and occupational information. The second part included a scale measuring the importance of electronic communication among extension workers in using AI programs and applications in smart agriculture. The third part measured the electronic communication means most frequently used by extension workers in employing AI programs and applications. The fourth part measured the contribution of electronic communication to improving extension workers' efficiency in using AI programs and applications in smart agriculture. The fifth part contained 15 items measuring the major obstacles facing extension workers in using AI applications in smart agriculture. After establishing the face validity of the questionnaire, reliability was assessed using Cronbach's alpha, which reached 0.95. The study population consisted of extension workers in the Nineveh Directorate of Agriculture and its 32 agricultural divisions, totaling 256 extension workers. A simple random sample of 128 extension workers, representing approximately 50% of the population, was selected. The data were coded, tabulated, and analyzed using SPSS. The results showed that the level of importance of electronic communication among extension workers in using AI programs and applications in smart agriculture was moderate and tended toward high, with a percentage of 48%. The item "Using electronic platforms belonging to agricultural institutions to obtain information related to AI programs and applications" ranked first, with a mean of 4.34. The contribution of electronic communication to improving extension workers' efficiency in using AI programs and applications in smart agriculture was high, with a percentage of 46%. No significant differences were found in the importance of electronic communication according to gender or training courses, whereas significant differences were reported according to educational qualification, years of occupational service, level of Internet use, and willingness to use social networking sites concerning smart-agriculture technologies. The item "Poor compatibility of some AI applications with the nature and needs of agricultural extension work in Nineveh Governorate" was identified as the most important obstacle. The major recommendation was for the Ministry of Agriculture to establish or develop official agricultural electronic platforms affiliated with agricultural and extension institutions and containing updated information on AI applications and their use in different agricultural fields. The main proposed future study was to investigate the obstacles to using AI applications in agricultural extension work in Nineveh Governorate from the perspective of extension workers.

items.title: The information professional as an ethical intermediary: information quality criteria and the ethics of generative AI
items.abstract: Introduction. The adoption of generative AI raises ethical concerns for information professionals whose intermediary role requires them to ensure information quality standards that users cannot independently verify. Professional ethics address quality superficially, and the ethical implications of generative AI have not been examined from the perspective of professional obligations. Method. A scoping review assessed 644 records across three search strands, retaining 120 papers, which were analysed against ten information quality criteria and assessed for the strength of their ethical framing. Analysis. Ten practice-derived quality criteria, corresponding closely to ISO/IEC 25012, are shown to be based on a Kantian deontological framework complemented by a Marxist treatment of algorithmic surplus value. For each criterion the literature documenting the relevant AI failure mode is reviewed and its ethical treatment assessed. Results. Four criteria, accuracy, objectivity, identifiable origin, and accessibility, attract substantial ethical attention. For the remaining six, ethical treatment is limited or absent. Conclusions. The information professional's intermediary role is an ethical necessity. Professional organisations are called upon to lobby actively for AI governance using the criteria framework developed here.

items.title: THE INTEGRATION OF DIGITAL PEDAGOGY AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN MODERN HIGHER EDUCATION: STRATEGIES, CHALLENGES, AND FUTURE OUTLOOK
items.abstract: This scientific thesis examines the transformative impact of digital pedagogy and artificial intelligence (AI) integration within modern higher education systems. As educational paradigms shift from traditional instructor-centric models toward personalized, technology-enhanced learning environments, understanding the pedagogical, methodological, and psychological implications becomes critical. The study evaluates adaptive learning platforms, digital assessment tools, and AI-driven instructional scaffolding across diverse academic contexts. Employing a mixed-methods approach comprising empirical classroom surveys, literature synthesis, and qualitative faculty interviews, the research highlights key drivers of student engagement, academic performance retention, and critical thinking development. The findings demonstrate a 28% increase in conceptual retention when digital interactive tools are combined with active learning frameworks. However, significant challenges persist, including digital inequality, algorithmic bias, and the potential degradation of human-to-human pedagogical rapport. The paper concludes with actionable recommendations for curriculum designers, institutional policymakers, and educators aiming to establish an ethically sound, technologically robust educational ecosystem.

items.abstract: Title:The IU Design White Paper V101.1: An Energy-Anchored Second Monetary System for the AI Economy Authors: Zhifeng Zu, Wei Xiong (with AI collaboration — see disclosure) Abstract:The incumbent monetary and accounting system cannot carry the AI economy: compute investment appears on balance sheets as losses, token consumption evaporates from cost accounting, and broad-liability growth in major economies now systematically outpaces asset-recognition growth (China Δg≈+9.2%/yr; US Δg≈+2.7%/yr), implying a wall-impact window of 5.4–9.3 years for the incumbent ledger. This white paper specifies IU (Intelligence Unit), a sovereignly issued second currency anchored to verified AI energy throughput (1 IU ≡ 1 kWh of verified effective throughput, nominal anchor), running in parallel with fiat. The specification covers: ontology (a flow anchor, not a stock anchor — minting against verified throughput, burning on use); issuance (dual verification of meter readings against token output, a quality-coefficient basket, two-stage pricing from accounting price to call auction); circulation (three channels — intra-industry settlement, a fiat exchange gate, cross-border mutual recognition — plus token futures and a closed-loop supply identity); governance (a Second Central Bank holding the issuance key, human-held settlement finality); seven failure modes with circuit breakers; and the conditions of the system's own disappearance. All parameters are back-derived from a five-variable collapse engine validated against 150 years of five historical crises, and are fully reproducible. This document is the specification layer of the forthcoming book The Wealth Format of the AI Era and the Ultimate Concession (working title). items.title: The Pemberdayaan Komunitas Kreatif Kampung Batik Semarang Melalui Edukasi AI Motif Batik Berbasis Kearifan Lokal
items.abstract: This community service program aims to empower batik artisans, particularly female MSMEs in Kemijen and Kampoeng Batik Semarang, by educating them on utilizing Artificial Intelligence (AI) as an assistive technology to design Semarangan batik motifs based on local wisdom. An interdisciplinary team spanning Communication Science, Cultural Studies, English, and Visual Communication Design implemented this program. The execution methods included conceptual counseling, practical training on generative AI, project-based creative mentoring, and design evaluations. The results demonstrated a significant increase in digital literacy: 100% of participants understood AI's role as an assistive design tool, and practical AI operational skills rose to 86%. The program successfully produced more than 5 collaborative batik motif prototypes (e.g., Warak Ngendog, blekok, and tamarind tree) and digital promotion copywriting in English. Program outputs include an ISBN-registered interdisciplinary educational module, an Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) registration draft for the educational model, and a scientific article draft submitted to a national Sinta 5 accredited journal. In conclusion, utilizing AI as an assistive technology accelerates visual design exploration without diluting local cultural philosophy and authenticity, thereby strengthening the economic resilience and digital capacity of female batik MSMEs in the creative industry. Keywords--- Artificial Intelligence (AI), Semarangan Batik, female MSMEs, local wisdom, community empowerment.

items.title: The Philosophical Counselor in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: From Practice to Profession, from Profession to Algorithm
items.abstract: The paper addresses the ethical integration of artificial intelligence into philosophical counseling in Romania. We begin with the criteria used by Julia Clare and Richard Sivil to distinguish between practice and profession, and with the roadmap for recognizing the new profession of philosophical counseling in Romania, outlined in 2019 by Vasile Hațegan. Much of this process has already been accomplished; what remains is the cognitive dimension, which has yet to catch up with either online or algorithmically assisted practice. In the second part of the article, we draw upon Hațegan’s comparisons between philosophical counseling and psychotherapy, coaching, spiritual counseling, and mediation to identify five distinguishing criteria: counselor neutrality, the relational nature of the process, non-dependency, the non-therapeutic nature of the practice, and client autonomy. We treat these criteria as an ethical test for conversational AI agents. The APPAgpt platform proves particularly useful in this endeavor; through it, the American Philosophical Practitioners Association invites the public to converse with bots simulating dialogues with great thinkers, while simultaneously emphasizing the importance of the human counselor. The test yields nuanced results. When used by the counselor as a tool, artificial intelligence can operate within the boundaries of the practice; however, when placed in the counselor's role facing the client, it exceeds those limits. The article concludes with proposals for future occupational standards and the philosophical counselor's code of ethics: the inclusion of a competency unit dedicated to digitally mediated practice, as well as a decision-making procedure inspired by Henk van Luijk’s model.

items.title: The prevalence of asthma and pneumoconiosis among dental professionals and technicians: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract: With the increasing use of dental services and the consequent rise in the use of various materials, the prevalence of respiratory disorders and respiratory symptoms associated with these chemicals and pollutants has increased. Therefore, in this systematic review and meta-analysis, we aim to evaluate the prevalence of asthma and pneumoconiosis among dental professionals and technicians. A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Clarivate analytics databases. Based on the PRISMA checklist (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses), first the title and abstract and after that the full-text of retrieved studies were screened and relevant studies were included. The required data was extracted from the studies. To assess the quality of studies, the Newcastle-Ottawa scale checklist was used. Heterogeneity between included studies was measured using the I-square statistic. To examine the possibility of publication bias, the Egger’s test and funnel plot were used and sensitivity analysis was also performed. Thirty studies (10 studies on asthma and 20 studies on pneumoconiosis) were included in the meta-analysis. A total of 7,603 people were included in the analysis of asthma prevalence. The results of the meta-analysis showed that the prevalence of asthma among dental professionals and technicians was 6.9% (95% confidence interval (CI): 4.9-8.9%). A total of 2790 people were included in the analysis of pneumoconiosis. The results of a meta-analysis of studies revealed that the prevalence of pneumoconiosis among dental professionals and technicians was 19.8% (95%CI: 15.2-24.5%). The observed prevalence of asthma and pneumoconiosis among dental professionals and technicians is substantial and raises concerns regarding their occupational respiratory health. These findings highlight the importance of appropriate preventive measures, occupational health monitoring, and further research to better characterize respiratory risks in this population.

items.title: The Reflection Penalty: when managers accept leadership coaching from a human but not an AI agent
items.abstract: Leadership coaching develops managers but is expensive and difficult to scale. AI may be able to help scale access, but “answering machine” like AI coaching agents invite cognitive offloading and weaken learning. We instantiated a human coaching protocol, supported across prior cycles, as a text-based AI coach built to prompt reflective questioning. In the fourth cycle of a design-based research program at a global consulting firm, eight managers received the same protocol from a human coach and the AI coach, applied each session in an observed onboarding activity, and reflected on both in interviews. All eight welcomed the probing questions and preferred the human coach. Notably, they resisted the same protocol of questioning from the AI coach and wanted answers from it instead. This study’s theoretical contribution is the Reflection Penalty, the cost an AI coach pays for asking a user to do the reflective work that makes human coaching effective. Its practical contribution is a jobs-to-be-done map for AI coaching, assembled from proposals participants raised on their own. It divides coaching into distinct jobs and assigns each to the human or the AI best suited to it. Both contributions are offered to those designing AI tools that aim to support reflection

items.title: THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN INTRINSIC, EXTRINSIC MOTIVATION AND ACADEMIC ACHIEVEMENT AMONG NCE STUDENTS OF FCT COLLEGES OF EDUCATION, ABUJA
items.abstract: This study examined the relationship between intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation and academic achievement among NCE students of FCT College of Education, Abuja. A correlational survey research design was adopted, as the study sought to determine the extent and direction of the relationship among intrinsic, extrinsic motivation and students’ academic achievement. The population comprised 1,704 NCE II students, from which a sample of 313 students was drawn using the Krejcie and Morgan (1970) table and stratified and simple random sampling techniques was used in selecting the respondents fairly. A total of 311 questionnaires, representing 99.5% of the sampled respondents, were correctly completed and returned. Data were collected using a researcher-developed 30-item structured questionnaire divided into three sections: students’ cumulative grade point average (CGPA), 15 items measuring intrinsic motivation, and 15 items measuring extrinsic motivation. The instrument was face and content validated by experts, yielding a validity index of 0.76, and its reliability was established through a pilot study using Cronbach’s Alpha, which yielded coefficients of 0.93 and 0.88 for intrinsic and extrinsic motivation respectively. Data were analysed using Pearson Product Moment Correlation at the 0.05 level of significance. The findings revealed a weak to moderate, positive and significant relationship between intrinsic and extrinsic motivation (r = .385, p < .05); a strong, positive and significant relationship between intrinsic motivation and academic achievement (r = .764, p < .05); and a strong, positive and significant relationship between extrinsic motivation and academic achievement (r = .629, p < .05). Consequently, the three null hypotheses were rejected. The study concluded that both intrinsic and extrinsic motivation are significantly associated with academic achievement. It was recommended that lecturers and school authorities design tasks that are interesting and engaging, employ inquiry-based and student-centred teaching methods, and clearly communicate the career benefits of academic success to enhance student motivation and performance.

items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has already forced colleges and universities to rewrite their academic integrity policies. Now it's forcing a harder, equally technical conversation in disability services. Students with documented disabilities are beginning to request generative AI tools as part of their accommodation plans. Many existing accommodation policies do not address these technologies. Campus administrators must address these novel questions now to meet legal obligations under disability law while maintaining their institution's academic standards.

items.title: The Role of Agentic Instruction Categories for Code Generation: A Study of Five Python Libraries
items.abstract: Agentic coding systems increasingly rely on repository-level agent files, such as AGENTS.md, to communicate project knowledge and developer intent. However, it remains unclear which categories of agent instructions enable efficient agent-file generation and accurate code generation. We evaluate five instruction categories: Repository Overview, Function Description, Implementation Detail, Testing, and Reconstruction Steps, across all 31 non-empty combinations using two Large Language Models (LLMs), Gemma 4 and GPT-5.4, and five human-written Python libraries. Our study addresses two research questions, comprising five sub-questions, on agent file generation and code generation. Results show that the number of instructions alone does not determine token usage for agent-file generation, with substantial variation across models and libraries. Although most AI-generated libraries compiled successfully regardless of the instruction combination, functional correctness remained limited. No Gemma 4 variant passed all tests, whereas 12.99% of GPT-5.4 variants did. Function Description achieved Gemma 4's highest partial-pass rate, while Reconstruction Steps achieved GPT-5.4's highest full-pass rate. For structural similarity to human-written code, Reconstruction Steps was most frequently associated with libraries closest to the originals in Lines of File and total Cyclomatic Complexity, while Testing and Reconstruction Steps were jointly most frequent for File Count and Function Count.

items.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Administrative Decision-Making in Iraq: Digital Transformation as a Model
items.abstract: This research aims to examine the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in enhancing the quality and efficiency of administrative decision-making in Iraq, adopting digital transformation as both an analytical model and an integrated practical framework. The study focuses on the readiness of Iraqi government institutions to adopt intelligent systems and the impact of these technologies on improving decision-making speed and transparency, reducing human error, and fostering a work environment grounded in data and intelligent analysis. The research employs a descriptive-analytical approach to review concepts related to AI and digital transformation, an inductive approach to infer relationships between variables, and a field-based approach involving the analysis of government documents and reports. Content analysis tools were also utilized to assess the extent to which AI applications—such as predictive systems, decision-support algorithms, chatbots, and big data analytics tools—are being employed. The findings indicate that the implementation of AI within Iraqi public administration remains in its early stages, despite official moves toward digitalization. Key opportunities identified include faster decision-making, increased transparency, reduced human intervention in routine tasks, and the creation of reliable databases to support planning and policymaking. Challenges include weak digital infrastructure, limited technical skills among staff, the absence of a legal framework regulating artificial intelligence applications, and poor integration between government systems. The research recommends formulating a comprehensive national strategy for artificial intelligence, developing digital infrastructure, upskilling government personnel, strengthening partnerships with the private sector and academic institutions, and updating legislation to align with digital governance and privacy protection standards, thereby ensuring a secure and effective environment for the adoption of smart technologies.

items.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Spatio-Temporal Analysis of Rural Transformation
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Rural transformation - the multidimensional transition of demographic, economic, social, spatial, technological, environmental and institutional conditions in rural areas has traditionally been studied through periodic surveys, census decadal enumeration and retrospective mapping. This paper investigates whether artificial intelligence (AI) can fundamentally transform this analytical paradigm from retrospective description toward continuous, predictive and anticipatory spatio-temporal intelligence. Through a critical synthesis of the emerging GeoAI literature, analysis of primary Indian and international datasets, and development of an original conceptual framework-the AI-Enabled SpatioTemporal Rural Transformation Framework (AI-STRF) this paper argues that AI is not merely improving existing rural research techniques but may be creating a new paradigm of rural geographical analysis. The paper examines AI applications across demographic, agricultural, infrastructural, environmental and socioeconomic dimensions of rural change, identifies critical research gaps, and constructs evidence-based 2030-2050 future scenarios. It concludes that while AI offers transformative potential for predictive rural geography, realisation of this potential depends critically on addressing data inequality, algorithmic bias, institutional capacity, and the fundamental distinction between prediction and causal explanation. The future of rural geography, this paper contends, lies not in replacing human geographical expertise but in augmenting it through intelligent, ethically governed spatio-temporal analysis.

items.title: The Role of Digital Leadership and Artificial Intelligence in Sustainable Tourism Strategies: Evidence from Turkey
items.abstract: This study investigates how digital leadership and artificial intelligence (AI) contribute to the development of sustainable tourism strategies, focusing on the context of the Turkish hospitality industry. The central research question examines how digital leadership practices guide the strategic use of AI technologies toward sustainability-oriented outcomes. Grounded in digital leadership theory and the triple bottom line sustainability framework, the study adopts a qualitative multiple case study design. Data were collected through document analysis of sustainability reports, strategic plans, and publicly available digital transformation materials from four leading hotel groups in Turkey: Rixos Hotels, Titanic Hotels, Maxx Royal Hotels, and The Marmara Hotels. The data were analyzed using thematic analysis to identify recurring patterns and strategic practices. The findings reveal that AI-enabled applications support sustainability by enhancing operational efficiency, enabling personalized service delivery, and improving environmental management practices, particularly in areas such as energy efficiency, resource optimization, and carbon footprint reduction. Furthermore, the results indicate that the alignment of digital leadership with ethical responsibility, innovation orientation, and employee digital capability development strengthens organizational competitiveness and long-term sustainability. The study contributes to the literature by offering an applied strategic framework that conceptualizes digital leadership as a governance mechanism directing AI technologies toward sustainability objectives. Beyond academic contributions, the findings provide practical insights for managers and policymakers seeking to integrate digital transformation initiatives with sustainable tourism strategies, especially in emerging tourism economies.

items.title: The Tensed Computer Improviser and the workmanship of risk: Small-dataset machine learning and real-time interactive musical improvisation
items.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has entered music overwhelmingly by way of large industrial models trained on vast corpora, in which the outcome is fixed in advance by an apparatus that the musician neither controls nor understands. This article argues that the essential machine-learning operations of dataset assembly, feature extraction and model fitting can instead be utilised transparently as part of an artist’s creative practice. Looking to David Pye’s concepts of workmanship of certainty and workmanship of risk , this article examines the design of the Tensed Computer Improviser (TCI), an open-source machine improviser built in Max with the Fluid Corpus Manipulation (FluCoMa) toolkit, which trains models from a small audio corpus of the user’s own choosing, with no pretrained component and no external training stage. Situating the TCI within a genealogy of machine improvisation using small data, the article analyses its design through the vocabulary of craft where the corpus curation and training are integrated into the creative act and the characteristic errors of small data are welcomed as tool-marks.

items.title: The Use of Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Post-Reading Presentations in Improving Secondary School Students’ Attitudes Towards Developing Turkish Vocabulary
items.abstract: The aim of this study is to examine whether middle school students’ attitudes toward developing Turkish vocabulary differ according to the tools they preferred during the preparation of post-reading presentations. The study employed a quantitative comparative correlational design. The participants consisted of 56 fifth-grade students attending a public middle school in Burhaniye, Balıkesir, Türkiye. Within the framework of the Türkiye Century Education Model, students presented the books they had read by using artificial intelligence-supported tools, conventional digital tools, or hand-prepared materials, based on their own preferences. No intervention was made in the natural learning environment. After the presentations, the Attitude Scale for Developing Vocabulary in the Turkish Course, developed by Yaşar and Topçuoğlu Ünal (2016), was administered. Descriptive statistics and the independent-samples t-test were used for data analysis. The findings revealed that students who preferred artificial intelligence-supported tools obtained significantly higher attitude scores toward developing Turkish vocabulary than those who preferred conventional digital tools or hand-prepared materials. The calculated effect size (Cohen’s d ≈ 0.59) indicated a medium effect. The results suggest that students’ attitudes toward developing Turkish vocabulary differ significantly according to the tools they preferred during the preparation of post-reading presentations.

items.title: The Utilization of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Technology in Islamic Religious Education to Develop Students’ Spiritual Character at MTs Diniyyah Putri Lampung, Gedong Tataan District, Pesawaran Regency, Lampung Province
items.abstract: This study aims to examine the utilization of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Islamic Religious Education (IRE) and its contribution to strengthening students’ spiritual character at MTs Diniyyah Putri Lampung, Pesawaran Regency, Lampung Province. The study was motivated by the challenges of providing relevant and engaging Islamic Religious Education for a digitally oriented generation, whose familiarity with technology is not always accompanied by strong spiritual awareness. This research employed a qualitative approach with a case study design. The informants included the Head of the Madrasah, IRE teachers, students, dormitory Ummi, and PMDL administrators. Data were collected through in-depth interviews, participatory observations, and documentation of IRE learning activities. The findings indicate that AI was utilized through several applications, including AI-based chatbots to facilitate students’ religious inquiries and spiritual guidance, interactive digital applications to support dhikr and self-reflection (muhasabah), and visual-based AI learning platforms to present Islamic Religious Education materials in a more engaging manner. These applications supported interactive religious learning, encouraged students to reflect on their behavior and religious practices, increased learning motivation, and strengthened emotional engagement with Islamic learning. However, the findings also demonstrate that AI has a supportive rather than substitutive role in spiritual character formation. Teachers remain essential in modeling and cultivating values such as sincerity, patience, discipline, and closeness to Allah SWT through direct guidance and interpersonal interaction. The novelty of this study lies in identifying AI as a complementary pedagogical instrument that connects digital Islamic learning with students’ spiritual self-reflection, while emphasizing the irreplaceable role of teachers in authentic spiritual character formation. This study contributes to the development of technology-integrated Islamic Religious Education by proposing a balanced approach in which AI supports learning innovation without displacing teacher-mediated spiritual formation.

items.title: The world’s oldest living culture leads the way with interpretable generative AI: Aboriginal women shaping the future of perinatal mental health services
items.abstract: Despite their strengths, Aboriginal mothers experience significant health disparities, including perinatal mental health challenges influenced by social, historical, and cultural determinants. Routine risk screening informs follow-up care, yet conventional approaches often fail to address cultural considerations. The Baby Coming You Ready (BCYR) program provides a strengths-based, culturally adapted digital assessment designed to enhance perinatal mental health care. However, some clinicians continue to rely primarily on conventional risk scores, which can neglect broader contextual circumstances influencing Aboriginal mothers, including cultural strengths and protective factors, thereby limiting the program’s full impact. This exploratory model-development study examined whether generative AI data augmentation combined with an intrinsically interpretable machine-learning model could support culturally contextualised prediction of perinatal psychological distress among Aboriginal mothers. We analysed deidentified BCYR pilot data from 293 Aboriginal mothers across six Western Australian sites. After excluding five records with incomplete outcome data, the analytic dataset included 288 participants. Models were evaluated using repeated internal train-test splits, with synthetic data used only for training augmentation and performance assessed on held-out real test data. The highest internal performance was observed for the TVAE-augmented Explainable Boosting Machine at an augmentation ratio of 1.0, with an accuracy of 0.867, an F1 score of 0.817, and an AUC of 0.934. Model explanations identified self-blame, loneliness, family pride, day-to-day management, sleep, and related contextual factors as influential contributors to model-estimated risk. These explanations are intended as prompts for culturally safe discussion and clinical reflection. Findings suggest that interpretable generative AI may have potential to support culturally responsive perinatal mental health assessment. However, broader community-governed external validation and prospective clinical workflow evaluation are required before clinical implementation.

items.title: Theorising Prompt Humanities: Human–AI Interpretation and Postcolonial Knowledge in Amitav Ghosh's The Calcutta Chromosome
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has made prompting a prominent mode of interaction between users and large language models, but prompting is not exhausted by its technical role in eliciting model outputs. This article proposes Prompt Humanities as an interdisciplinary interpretive framework for examining prompts as rhetorical, hermeneutic, and culturally situated acts. Drawing on philosophical hermeneutics, reader-response criticism, speech-act theory, poststructuralism, Digital Humanities, and postcolonial studies, the framework asks how prompt-mediated interaction reframes questions of interpretation, authorship, dialogue, and knowledge production. The framework is developed through a qualitative close reading of Amitav Ghosh's The Calcutta Chromosome. Rather than claiming that Ghosh predicted contemporary generative AI, the article treats the novel retrospectively as a literary site in which recursive questioning, fragmented archives, distributed forms of knowledge, and computer-mediated inquiry can be compared with prompt-mediated interpretation. The analysis focuses on Murugan's revisionary hypotheses, Mangala's counter-scientific network, Antar's interactions with the digital system Ava, and the novel's persistent resistance to epistemological closure. The article argues that Prompt Humanities can complement existing Digital Humanities and postcolonial approaches by making the prompt itself an object of literary and cultural analysis. Its contribution is therefore not the claim that prompting has been absent from humanities scholarship, but the development of a specific integrative vocabulary for analysing how questions, responses, archives, and interpretive agents are organised in human–AI and literary contexts. The framework is presented as provisional and transferable, requiring further testing across texts, languages, genres, and forms of human–AI interaction.

items.title: Thinking With, Not Through, AI: Philosophical Counseling and Ethical Self-Authorship in Teacher Education
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly used to interpret professional situations, formulate arguments, and consider responses to ethical dilemmas. Although these systems can broaden reflection, their persuasive outputs may encourage moral outsourcing, defined as transferring substantive elements of ethical interpretation, justification, or judgment to an external system without adequate examination, endorsement, or responsibility. This conceptual article asks how generative AI can be integrated into philosophical counseling and ethical reflection in teacher education without undermining ethical self-authorship. Drawing on philosophical counseling, moral development, relational autonomy, professional ethics, and AI literacy, it develops the Ethical Self-Authorship Cycle. The model comprises five iterative stages: articulating the dilemma, pluralizing perspectives, interrogating assumptions, testing reasons and consequences, and reclaiming moral authorship. Its contribution is threefold. First, it distributes deliberative functions between the human participant and AI by specifying what the system may contribute and what it cannot establish at each stage. Second, it requires the process to conclude with a human-formulated justification rather than an AI-generated recommendation. Third, it treats ethical self-authorship as a developing capacity requiring pedagogical scaffolding and ethically and digitally prepared teacher educators. An illustrative case demonstrates the model’s application to a dilemma involving student use of AI in assessment. The article argues that AI may generate material for ethical inquiry, but it cannot represent affected people, determine which values should prevail, or assume professional responsibility. Moral authorship and answerability must remain human.

items.title: TimeCap: A Scalable Open-Source Pipeline for Captioning Wearable Health Time-Series Data
items.abstract: Time-series data generated continuously across industrial, environmental, and especially health domains produce multimodal signals whose scale and heterogeneity make their processing and interpretation particularly challenging. Time-Series Language Models (TSLMs) promise scalable interpretation of these signals, yet remain bottlenecked by a fundamental lack of text-annotated time series pairs that are signal-grounded, reproducible, and extensible across modalities and schemas. Existing paired corpora are either closed or limited in scale and modality coverage. Annotation with large language models could scale them up, but its outputs cannot be regenerated exactly, which prevents others from re-deriving, extending, or auditing the resulting corpus. To address this, we release TimeCap, an open deterministic captioning pipeline with three reusable extractor tiers and a cross-channel synthesis layer that operates directly on the signal with no language model in the loop, extensible to new schemas by writing channel definitions alone. This positions TimeCap as a reproducible mechanism for future dataset generation rather than a one-off release. Applying TimeCap to OpenMHC, the MyHeart Counts wearable dataset, yields MHCap, the largest open caption layer for multimodal wearable time-series data. MHCap spans 19 Apple HealthKit channels and 7,005,763 captions over 908,944 person-days. To showcase the impact of the corpus, we train OpenTSLM, a time-series language model, on MHCap and benchmark on health-outcome prediction. Caption-augmented training (OpenTSLM-Cap) outperforms a label-only baseline on 29 of 32 per-user binary evaluations across 8 tasks.

items.title: Toward a Civil Security Orientation: Bridging Research and Practice in Homeland Security and Emergency Management. Insights from the 2nd Pracademic Emergency Management and Homeland Security Summit
items.abstract: Abstract This article synthesizes proceedings and outcomes from the 2nd Pracademic Emergency Management and Homeland Security Summit, hosted virtually by Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University’s Worldwide Campus College of Arts & Sciences and its Virtual Collaboratory for Security and Resilience Education, Research, and Engagement. Drawing on contributions from an international and interdisciplinary group of scholars, practitioners, students, policymakers, and professional organizations representing higher education, government, industry, and operational practice, the summit examined emerging challenges and future directions across homeland security, emergency management, resilience, public health, homeland defense, disaster planning, information disorder, artificial intelligence, ethics, and standards development. Several cross-cutting findings emerged. First, preparedness and resilience increasingly require adaptive, inclusive, and whole-community approaches grounded in trusted communication, social capital, functional needs inclusion, and meaningful stakeholder engagement. Second, while artificial intelligence, remote sensing, and advanced decision-support systems offer substantial operational promise, their implementation demands stronger attention to ethical oversight, interoperability, governance, and consensus-based standards capable of translating technical capability into operational relevance. Third, increasingly complex threat environments reinforce the need for critical thinking, scenario-based learning, ethical reasoning, and career-long professional development to prepare leaders to operate across institutional boundaries and under incomplete information.

items.title: Towards a New Learning Ecology: The Mediator Role of Teachers Facing Generative AI in the University Context of Peru, Chile, and Colombia
items.abstract: Background The emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has created an ontological disruption in higher education, challenging traditional pedagogical mediation and academic production. This study examines the transformation of the teaching role in university environments across Peru, Chile, and Colombia, addressing a knowledge gap in Latin American empirical research regarding faculty perceptions and daily practices with Large Language Models. Methods The research employed a descriptive-interpretative qualitative design with an open-ended survey approach interpreted through a hermeneutic lens. A non-probabilistic sample of 48 undergraduate and graduate professors from 20 Higher Education Institutions in the region participated. Data were collected through a validated 18-item structured online questionnaire and analyzed using Reflexive Thematic Analysis assisted by Atlas.ti software. Results The findings identify a transition from traditional instructional roles toward a “mediator-curator” model, where educators act as orchestrators of human-AI co-intelligence. Key applications include pedagogical re-engineering, such as dynamic curricular design, Socratic tutoring, and the shift from product-oriented to process-oriented assessment. Critical dimensions emerged regarding the need for pedagogical re-engineering, ethical challenges in academic integrity, and the development of critical AI literacy. National variations showed Chile focusing on pedagogical equity, Colombia on research productivity, and Peru on didactic agility. Conclusions The integration of GenAI in the Latin American university context requires a situated pedagogical response that transcends instrumental use. The study proposes a new learning ecology where the teacher facilitates critical interaction between students and generative systems. This shift necessitates a reconfiguration of teaching competencies toward epistemic curation and algorithmic responsibility to ensure meaningful and ethical learning.

items.title: Towards Continual Learning: Mitigating Forgetting With Subspace Tuning
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) acquire new skills through fine-tuning, but it can destroy capabilities they already have: catastrophic forgetting remains a central obstacle to continual learning in LLMs. Recent works connect forgetting to how far, and along which directions, fine-tuning moves the weights. On-policy methods such as reinforcement learning and on-policy distillation avoid updating the principal singular directions of weight matrices and thus forget less. In contrast, SFT concentrates updates along these directions and is susceptible to catastrophic forgetting. In this work, we introduce Subspace Tuning (SST), which restricts each weight update to the bottom singular subspace, eliminating changes along the principal directions. SST is optimizer-agnostic and composes well with fine-tuning recipes including SFT and self-distillation. SST combines tight subspace protection, dense gradient estimation, and a simple refresh mechanism, enabling stronger learning than prior orthogonal fine-tuning methods. With these mechanisms, protecting as much as 99\% of the weight subspace substantially improves retention while preserving strong target-task performance. This behavior strengthens with model and data size and nearly eliminates forgetting in the large-model regime. SST also keeps the model close to its base distribution, inducing $2$--$4\times$ less KL drift than the baseline recipes. Overall, SST advances the learning--forgetting Pareto frontier, making it a practical default for fine-tuning pre-trained language models.

items.title: TRACER: A Multimodal Harness for Patient Care in Hospitals
items.abstract: Continuous video and clinical records provide complementary information for understanding how patient behavior evolves over a hospital stay. A central challenge is how to represent behavior across the entire stay while preserving access to fine-grained visual and clinical evidence. We introduce TRACER, a training-free multimodal harness that constructs minute-level action records from video and combines them with clinical records into hourly reports. The harness equips an LLM agent with tools to query this hierarchy, inspect relevant video, and retrieve clinical records. To evaluate TRACER, we construct two benchmarks. The first contains 397 annotated one-minute clips spanning 15 atomic actions; the second poses 144 clinician-informed multiple-choice questions, grounded in 264 hours of video and clinical records from two ICU patients. TRACER achieves up to 84.8% accuracy for action detection and 61.0% QA accuracy versus 49.3% for the strongest baseline using the same backbone. Across 280 patients spanning approximately 60,000 camera-hours, TRACER identifies significantly less purposeful activity in patients with a positive delirium assessment during their stay than in those without (p < 0.0001). Our results show that combining continuous video with clinical records can support understanding of patient behavior over time and across patient cohorts without training on protected health data.

items.title: Training Reasoning Models to Generate Diverse Scientific Ideas
items.abstract: One of the first steps of a research pipeline is generating ideas. Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to automate this step, but most of this work optimizes the quality of individual ideas, while overlooking diversity. In our work, we study document-grounded ideation, focusing on increasing the diversity of LLM generated ideas and ensuring they are high quality. Given prior papers, a model must propose a set of ideas that are each high-quality and clearly distinct from one another, while also being grounded in the input documents. To optimize for this, we propose training with a set-level reinforcement learning objective. In our setup, in a single generation, the model writes K structured idea cards grounded in the source papers, and the set is scored jointly, where each idea's quality is weighted by its distance from the ideas written before it. This teaches the model to steer each new idea away from its predecessors. We show that our trained 8B model achieves higher creative utility (a measure combining quality and diversity) than Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-6 Astra on our contamination-free benchmark. In a pilot human study with four experts, our sets are judged as promising as Claude Opus 4.8's and contain marginally more unique ideas. When a coding agent runs proof-of-concept experiments on the ideas, our model's success@k is comparable to Claude Opus 4.8's, so we see that the added diversity does not cost any executability.
